messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Jason is a 39-year-old divorced construction worker who came to treatment after years of trying to keep his inner life narrowed down to what he could get through a shift. The event he returned to again and again involved a coworker’s death on a job site several years earlier. Jason had been working on a commercial build, high up on steel framing, when a man he knew well lost footing and fell. Jason saw it happen in a sequence of stark, frozen images that still come back to him that way now: the turn of the man’s body, the sudden emptiness where he had been standing, the unnatural position after impact. What has stayed with Jason is not a story he tells in a smooth way, but flashes. When the memory breaks through, it is “like pictures,” abrupt and complete. Along with the images come sensory details that make the moment feel close rather than past. He can catch the same metallic, dusty smell of the site mixed with the sharper odor that was present after the fall, and at times he notices the taste that was in his mouth that day, the grit and bitterness he remembers as if it were happening again.

In the weeks after the accident, Jason did what seemed to make the most sense to him: he shut himself down and went back to work. He had come to believe that there was no point in letting himself feel much of anything, especially anger. Anger seemed dangerous, useless, and close to something he would not be able to control, so he never allowed himself to feel or express it. When coworkers complained about safety shortcuts or cursed about deadlines, Jason would go quiet. At home, after his divorce, the same pattern hardened. He kept his face flat, told people he was fine, and treated any stirring of rage or protest as something to choke off immediately.

At the same time, his understanding of the world had changed in a way he described as total. Before, construction had felt risky but governed by rules, skill, and experience. Since the accident, he was certain those beliefs had been destroyed. In his mind, terrible things did not wait for carelessness or bad judgment; they could happen in an instant, to anyone, with no warning and no real way to stop them. He was left with a deep sense of helplessness that extended beyond the site. If a man could die in front of him in the middle of a normal workday, then bad things were always already on their way. Alongside that was a quieter but equally painful conviction that he was inadequate. He did not describe this as guilt in elaborate terms; it came across more as a settled verdict on himself. Other men would have known what to do, would have prevented it, would have been stronger afterward. He believed he had failed some test he should have passed.

Over time, Jason developed ways of getting away from himself without calling attention to it. Some evenings he drove to casinos or placed bets because gambling gave him distraction and a jolt of excitement that cut through the deadened, constricted state he usually lived in. For a few hours, the spin of risk narrowed his mind to numbers, cards, and outcomes. At other times, especially after something at work brought the accident close, he deliberately tried to blank out. He described moments of making himself “leave” mentally, staring off until he felt far away from his body and surroundings. On active construction sites this had become particularly troubling. The clang of metal, the view from elevation, or catching an industrial smell in warm air could bring one of those visual bursts so sharply that he would mentally pull back from the scene around him. He was still showing up to work, but not in a way that felt steady or safe to him.

These habits had accumulated consequences. Gambling created financial strain that he kept hidden after the divorce, and his isolation deepened because he avoided situations where people might ask how he was doing or notice how checked out he had become. At work he had developed a reputation for being hard to read and distant. He took jobs and completed tasks, but he no longer trusted himself in the same easy, practiced way. What frightened him most was not just remembering the death; it was the sense that the world had become fundamentally unlivable, governed by catastrophe, and that he himself was not enough for it.

He finally sought help after a recent day on site when a smell carried him back so vividly that he could taste the grit in his mouth and found himself deliberately going blank while standing in the middle of a task. Nothing happened, but the fact that it could have was enough to shake him. Jason came in not because he felt hopeful exactly, but because he was running out of ways to outrun what he saw in those images. He said he wanted to know whether there was any way to live without feeling that disaster was always one second away, and without having to disappear from himself to make it through the day.
